title: Transfer on Death Deed in Texas Guide (September 2026)
summary: Learn how a Texas Transfer on Death Deed works, including filing steps, recording fees, and beneficiary rules. September 2026.
body_markdown:
A Texas Transfer on Death Deed (TODD) lets a property owner name a beneficiary to receive real estate at death, with no probate required. The owner keeps full control of the property during their lifetime, and the transfer only takes effect upon death. This guide covers key points for families and property owners to be aware of , including: what a TODD is and how it works, the requirements for a valid deed, how to file and what it costs, naming beneficiaries, how to revoke or change a TODD, tax matters, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- A Texas Transfer on Death Deed passes real estate to a named beneficiary at death, with no probate required.
- The deed must be signed, notarized, and recorded with the county clerk before the owner dies to have any legal effect.
- Recording fees generally run $25 to $40; a free PDF form is available through the Texas Transfer Toolkit.
- Estate creditors can reach property transferred by a TODD for up to two years after death; Lady Bird deeds carry no equivalent exposure.
- Elayne searches across financial accounts, unclaimed property registries, and life insurance sources to surface assets beyond the property a TODD already transferred.


## What Is a Transfer on Death Deed in Texas?


A[Transfer on Death Deed](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-a-transfer-on-death-deed-how-tod-deeds-help-you-skip-probate) (TODD) is a legal document that lets a Texas property owner name a beneficiary to receive real estate at death, with no probate required. The transfer only takes effect upon the owner's death; during their lifetime, nothing changes, and the owner retains full control, including the right to sell, mortgage, or revoke the deed at any time.

## How a Transfer on Death Deed Works in Texas


The owner signs and records the TODD while alive, but ownership stays exactly as it was throughout their lifetime. The owner can sell the property, take out a mortgage, lease it, or change their mind entirely. The named beneficiary has no current interest and no right to the property until death occurs.


At death, the transfer happens by operation of law, with no probate proceeding required for the beneficiary to take title. Understanding the difference between[probate vs. non-probate assets](https://www.elayne.com/resources/probate-vs-non-probate-assets) helps clarify why this distinction matters. If a will exists and contradicts the TODD, the TODD controls for that property.


The beneficiary's interest vests only at the moment of the owner's death, and only if the beneficiary survives the owner, a concept related to the[right of survivorship](https://www.elayne.com/resources/right-of-survivorship-wills-taxes-property) in inherited property. If the beneficiary predeceases the owner and no alternate was named, the transfer fails and the property falls back into the probate estate, raising questions about[real estate without a will](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-happens-to-real-estate-without-a-will) if no other planning is in place.


## Requirements for a Valid Transfer on Death Deed in Texas


For a TODD to be legally effective in Texas, it must satisfy each of these requirements under Chapter 114 of the Texas Estates Code:


- In writing, with the property identified by legal description
- Names at least one beneficiary
- Signed by the transferor (owner) and acknowledged before a notary public
- [Recorded with the county clerk](https://texaslawhelp.org/article/transfer-on-death-deeds-todds) in the county where the property is located prior to the owner's passing


## Where and How to File a Transfer on Death Deed in Texas


Filing happens at the county clerk's office in the county where the property sits. A deed for a Harris County home goes to the Harris County Clerk, a Travis County property goes to the Travis County Clerk, and so on.


Recording requires the original signed and notarized deed and payment of the recording fee. Fees generally run $25 to $40 for the first page, with a smaller per-page fee after that. Some counties also accept mail-in submissions.


## Naming Beneficiaries: Rules and Considerations


Multiple beneficiaries can be named on a single TODD, and each receives an equal share unless the deed specifies otherwise. A beneficiary does not sign the deed and has no obligation to accept the property at death. Beneficiaries can be a person, a charity, a trust, or another legal entity.


If a named beneficiary dies before the owner and no alternate is listed, that transfer lapses and the property falls back into the probate estate. Texas anti-lapse rules may apply in limited circumstances involving certain relatives.


## Rights as the Property Owner While the TODD Is in Effect


Signing a TODD changes nothing about how you own or use the property. The beneficiary receives no present interest and has no say over what happens while the owner is alive.


- Selling the property requires no consent from the beneficiary
- Refinancing or taking out a mortgage does not trigger a "due on sale" clause
- Homestead rights and ad valorem tax exemptions remain fully intact
- The deed can be revoked or rewritten at any time before death


A TODD is a recorded instruction, not a current transfer. The owner retains complete control until death.


## How to Cancel or Change a Transfer on Death Deed in Texas


Revoking or changing a TODD requires more than crossing out a name or adding new instructions to a will. The revocation must be a written, notarized instrument recorded with the same county clerk's office where the original TODD was filed, and it must happen before the owner's death.


A will alone cannot revoke a recorded TODD. Where a will and a TODD conflict, the TODD controls for that property.


## Pros and Cons of a Transfer on Death Deed in Texas


Advantages Drawbacks


Avoids probate entirely Two-year creditor clawback period after death


Owner retains full control and rights during life No title warranty passes to the beneficiary


No gift tax consequences Deed must be recorded before death or it has no effect


Homestead rights and tax exemptions stay intact Co-owned property can create complications


## What Happens After the Owner Dies: The Beneficiary's Next Steps


After the owner dies, the beneficiary must still take action to make the transfer official in the public record, and timing matters, since there are rules around[transferring property after death deadlines](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-long-do-you-have-to-transfer-property-after-death) .


To clear title, the beneficiary files an Affidavit of Death (sometimes called an Affidavit of Survivorship) along with[a certified copy of the death certificate](https://www.usa.gov/death-certificate) at the county clerk's office where the TODD was originally recorded. That recorded affidavit confirms the beneficiary's ownership in the public property records. Without it, the chain of title remains incomplete, and title companies will generally require these recorded documents before issuing title insurance for a sale or refinance.

## FAQ


### What is a Transfer on Death Deed in Texas, and how does it differ from a regular deed?


A Transfer on Death Deed (TODD) is a legal document under Chapter 114 of the Texas Estates Code that lets a property owner name a beneficiary to receive real estate at death, with no probate required. Unlike a standard deed, a Texas transfer on death deed transfers no current interest to the beneficiary. The owner keeps full control to sell, mortgage, or revoke the property at any time before death, and the beneficiary's interest only vests at the moment of the owner's death.


### Can a transfer on death deed in Texas be contested after the owner dies?


Yes. A TODD is a contestable instrument, meaning family members can challenge it in court if they believe the owner lacked mental capacity or was pressured into naming a specific beneficiary. Because a Texas transfer on death deed is prepared without court oversight, unlike a will, it can be more exposed to disputes after death. Working with a transfer on death deed lawyer in Texas can help reduce the risk of the deed failing or being challenged.


### How do I file a transfer on death deed in Texas, and what does it cost?


The Texas transfer on death deed form must be signed, notarized, and recorded with the county clerk in the county where the property sits before the owner dies. Recording fees generally run $25 to $40 for the first page, with a smaller per-page fee after that.


### What happens to the rest of the estate after a transfer on death deed transfers the house?


The TODD handles the real property, but financial accounts, retirement accounts, life insurance policies, and other assets transfer through separate processes that require their own discovery, notification, and administration steps.
